newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia foresees coffee output growth in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia foresees coffee output growth in 97/98.

text.p: Favourable weather and high world prices will boost Ethiopian coffee output in 1997/98, Ethiopian authorities said on Thursday.
They told Reuters Ethiopia's organic coffee, which required a negligible amount of fertiliser or pesticide to flourish, was flowering and the outlook for 1997/98 was very good.
"We are looking at a better crop. Production is going up," said Aster Estephanos, head of planning at the state Ethiopia Coffee and Tea Development Authority.
"The short rains are on time and we do not expect any problems with the weather. It is positive so far."
Aster said production normally averaged 250,000 tonnes.
Aster saw export receipts rising to more than $300 million in 1996/97 (July/June) from $279.5 million in 1995/96 owing to favourable prices on the international market.

She said prices of washed arabicas had reached $292 per 17-kg bag at end-February compared with $206 in July 1996. She quoted prices of dry coffees at $200 per 17-kg bag at end-February from $176 in July last year.

Coffee is sold per 17-kg bag at Ethiopia's daily coffee auctions in Addis Ababa and the town of Dire Dawa. But it is shipped in 60-kg bags. Aster said she saw no future changes in the auction sales system for the industry.
Private Ethiopian coffee expect to export up to 60,000 tonnes of a total 108,000 forecast for 1996/97.

Aster said between July 1996 and end-February, a total of 59,984 tonnes had been exported. She saw the export figure at around 70,000 tonnes by end-March and said Ethiopia would meet the 108,000 tonne export target.
She forecast exports rising to around 110,000 tonnes or more in 1997/98, in line with favourable market conditions.

Ethiopia exported 102,000 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96 and earned $279.5 million --- lower than the $300.9 million it received for exporting 78,420 tonnes of coffee in 1994/95 due to poor global price of the commodity.

Ethiopia's main coffee destinations are Germany, Saudi Arabia and the United States, and Aster said the country had raised its marketing drive for Scandinavian countries and central and eastern Europe.
Some 95 percent of Ethiopian coffee is produced by smallholders while state farms account for five percent. The exact area under coffee was not immediately available.

Aster also spoke of increased efforts to promote Ethiopian coffee on speciality markets, with plans to attend an exhibition in New Orleans in April and to participate at all other major exhibitions until the year 2001.
